title: These Planets Are Fluffier Than Cotton Candy!
summary: Picture a planet as big as Jupiter but so light it could float in water—if you could find a bathtub big enough! That's what astronomers just discovered: two "super-puff" planets named TOI-791 b and TOI-791 c. They're about 1,110 light-years away, which means the light we see from them started traveling over a thousand years ago. These planets are truly fluffy. TOI-791 b has a density of only 0.038 grams per cubic centimeter. That's less than cotton candy, which is about 0.05 grams per cubic centimeter! Jupiter, by comparison, is 1.33 grams per cubic centimeter—about 30 times denser. So how did they get so puffy? Scientists think they have huge atmospheres made of hydrogen and helium, like giant balloons. The planets orbit their star in a special dance: for every five orbits of the inner planet, the outer one completes three. This gravitational tug-of-war helped astronomers weigh them. Even cooler? Volunteers from the Planet Hunters TESS project first spotted these worlds in data from NASA's TESS satellite. Then telescopes in Antarctica watched their long transits—each over 11 hours—without interruption thanks to months of winter darkness. Only a handful of super-puff planets are known, and finding two in one system is super rare. Scientists hope future studies will reveal how these cosmic cotton candies formed.
why_it_matters: Discovering unusual planets like these reminds us that space is full of surprises, and you can even help find them through citizen science projects.

background_read: NASA’s TESS satellite (a spacecraft that looks for planets outside our solar system) has found thousands of new worlds.
The Planet Hunters TESS project lets volunteers from around the world help spot planets in TESS data.
Astronomers used telescopes in Antarctica (the icy continent at the South Pole) because its long winter nights let them watch planets for hours without the sun rising.
Article_Structure: WHO: A team of astronomers, including citizen scientists from the Planet Hunters TESS project and NASA.
WHAT: They found two “super-puff” planets, TOI-791 b and c, that are as big as Jupiter but extremely light and fluffy.
WHERE: The planets orbit a star about 1,110 light-years from Earth, and were studied from space by TESS and from Antarctica.
WHY: Scientists want to understand how planets can have such low density and what that means for how planets form.

perspectives.description: They are thrilled to find such rare objects, which make them rethink ideas about how planets form.
Volunteers prove that anyone, not just professionals, can help make big space discoveries.
In the future, stronger telescopes might reveal how these cotton-candy planets were created and if there are many more of them.
